formal_elements.meaning: A mark that moves across a surface. Can be thick, thin, loose or careful.
formal_elements.example: "I used a continuous line so the drawing feels fluid and quick."

formal_elements.meaning: How light or dark something is.
formal_elements.example: "Strong tonal contrast makes the face look dramatic."

formal_elements.meaning: Hue, brightness and how colours work together.
formal_elements.example: "The muted palette gives the piece a calm mood."

formal_elements.meaning: How a surface feels, or looks like it would feel.
formal_elements.example: "Layering PVA and tissue built up a rough, worn texture."

formal_elements.meaning: A flat, 2D area with an outline.
formal_elements.example: "I simplified the leaves into bold shapes."

formal_elements.meaning: A 3D object, or something that looks 3D.
formal_elements.example: "Shading around the edges gives the shell form."

formal_elements.meaning: The area around and between things (positive and negative space).
formal_elements.example: "The negative space makes the figure feel isolated."
"The repeated pattern creates rhythm across the page."

formal_elements.meaning: How everything is arranged on the page.
formal_elements.example: "I cropped the composition so the eye goes straight to the hands."

formal_elements.meaning: How big or small something is, compared to other things.
formal_elements.example: "Making the object huge changes how it feels."
"I wanted contrast between the soft fabric and the sharp metal."

technique_words.Drawing: mark-making, hatching, cross-hatching, blending, continuous line, blind contour, smudging, erasing into, observational drawing
technique_words.Paint: wash, impasto (thick paint), glazing (thin see-through layers), dry brush, wet-on-wet, sgraffito (scratching into it), layering
technique_words.Printmaking: monoprint, collagraph, lino print, drypoint, screen print, relief print, registration, edition, plate
technique_words.Collage & mixed media: collage, assemblage, image transfer, tearing, layering, stitching, wax resist, bleach, ink washes
technique_words.3D: maquette (small test model), armature (inner support), casting, carving, construction, modelling, joining, surface finish
technique_words.Photography & digital: cropping, focus, depth of field, exposure, double exposure, scanning, digital collage, photo manipulation
technique_words.Graphic communication: typography, layout, grid, hierarchy, legibility, colour palette, icon, branding, audience
technique_words.Fashion & textiles: silhouette, drape, toile (test garment), embellishment, embroidery, pleating, dyeing, print repeat, fabric manipulation

research_words.meaning: Things you made or collected first-hand: your own drawings, photos, objects, visits, sketches from life.
Things made by someone else: an artist's work, a book, a website, a film.
Finding out the story around a piece: when, where, why it was made, and what it was reacting to.
Collecting images, colours and textures to feed your ideas.

swaps.better: "The soft tones create a calm, gentle mood."
"I like how the torn edges make it feel fragile, because..."
"The ink bled more than I expected, so next I'll try..."
"The loose, gestural marks give it energy."
"The bold contrast grabs your attention straight away."
"I made an observational study of... to explore..."
"I think this piece is resolved because..."

stages.what: You try lots of materials and disciplines to find out what you love. This is where you are now.
You choose a specialism, such as Fine Art, 3D, Graphic Communication or Fashion/Textiles.
Your own self-directed project, start to finish. This decides your final grade.

marking_areas.plain: Do you understand where your work fits, and what you're aiming for?
marking_areas.show: Links to artists and designers, and what your aim is.

marking_areas.plain: Did you gather lots of different sources and actually use them?
marking_areas.show: Where each source came from and what it gave you.

marking_areas.plain: Are you building skills and trying lots of techniques?
marking_areas.show: What technique you used and how you did it.

marking_areas.plain: When something didn't work, did you try another way?
marking_areas.show: What went wrong and what you changed.

marking_areas.plain: Are you managing your own time and setting your own goals?
marking_areas.show: Plans, next steps, and what you'll try next.

marking_areas.plain: Do you look back honestly and make decisions?
marking_areas.show: What worked, what didn't, and why you chose what you chose.

marking_areas.plain: Is your work clear and nicely laid out?
marking_areas.show: Headings, labels and a tidy layout. Less writing, more clarity.

Artist research page: "I chose [artist] because their work connects to my theme through..."
"What stands out to me is the way they use..."
Experiment and test page: "This didn't go how I planned, but I discovered..."
Development page (moving ideas forward): "I changed the scale / colour / material because..."
Finished piece reflection: "My aim was to... I think I achieved this because..."
"If I did it again I would..."

checklist: Every page has at least one note on it.
Each artist I studied has my own opinion and a link to my work.
I've labelled primary and secondary research.
There are tests that didn't work, with notes on what I learned.
I've explained why I made my choices.
There are clear next steps throughout.
I've used proper art words (Part 1 has loads).
Pages are labelled and easy to follow.

cfpm.heading: Content (what)
cfpm.questions: What is it? What's it of? What's it about? Is there a message or story?
cfpm.starters: "This work shows..." "The subject is..." "I think it's about..."

cfpm.heading: Form (how it looks)
cfpm.questions: Colours? Lines? Shapes? Texture? How is it arranged? How big is it?
cfpm.starters: "The artist uses a [muted/vibrant] palette..." "The composition is..."

cfpm.heading: Process (how it's made)
cfpm.questions: What materials and techniques? How long might it take? Any steps you can see?
cfpm.starters: "It's made using..." "The surface looks like it was built up by..."

cfpm.heading: Mood (how it feels)
cfpm.questions: How does it make you feel? What atmosphere does it have? Why?
cfpm.starters: "It feels [calm/eerie/playful] because..." "The [colour/scale] creates a sense of..."

artist_page_recipe.what: Artist's name, dates, where they're from, and what they do (painter, designer...).
1 to 3 works, each labelled with title, date, and where you found the picture.
2 or 3 sentences in your own words. Only what matters to your project. No life story.
Analyse one work using Content, Form, Process, Mood.
What you honestly think, with a reason. It's fine to dislike something if you say why.
How it connects to your theme or your work so far.
Make something: a study, a technique test, or your own piece using their approach (next page).

responses.what: Recreate a small section to understand how they did it.
responses.example: Copy a 10cm patch of a painting to learn their brushwork.

responses.what: Use their method on your subject.
responses.example: Use their layering technique on your own photos.

responses.what: Change one thing: scale, colour, material or subject.
responses.example: Turn a flat painting into a 3D paper model.

responses.what: Mix two artists, or an artist and your own research.
responses.example: One artist's colour palette with another's mark-making.

theme_steps.what: 10 minutes. Write everything the theme makes you think of, including weird ones. Weird is good.
Primary research: draw and photograph real things. Start close to home.
One that clearly fits, one that's a bit unexpected. Part 3 shows you how to write about them.
Try the same idea in three different ways. Note what each one does.
Which bit excites you most? Follow that. You don't have to cover the whole theme.

themes.name: Identity
themes.meaning: Who you are and what shapes you: family, culture, interests, and how others see you.
questions: What objects say the most about you?
How is the online you different from the real-life you?
What do you show people, and what do you keep hidden?
Where do you come from, and does it show?

artists.name: Frida Kahlo
artists.note: Painter. Self-portraits packed with personal symbols.

artists.name: Cindy Sherman
artists.note: Photographer. Photographs herself as invented characters.

artists.name: Kehinde Wiley
artists.note: Painter. Puts modern sitters into poses from old portraits.

artists.name: Grayson Perry
artists.note: Ceramics and tapestry about class and identity.

artists.name: Yinka Shonibare
artists.note: Sculpture and textiles using Dutch wax print fabric to question culture.

themes.research: Mirror self-portraits, photos of objects in your room, family photos, your own handwriting.
themes.test: Draw yourself in three different materials. Layer a portrait over a photo of something meaningful.

themes.name: Natural Forms
themes.meaning: Shapes and patterns from nature: shells, plants, bones, seeds.
questions: What do things look like really close up?
How does nature repeat the same patterns?
What happens when a tiny natural form is made huge?
How do things grow, and how do they die back?

artists.name: Karl Blossfeldt
artists.note: Photographer. Plant close-ups that look like sculpture.

artists.name: Georgia O'Keeffe
artists.note: Painter. Huge close-up flowers and bones.

artists.name: Barbara Hepworth
artists.note: Sculptor. Smooth organic forms pierced with holes.

artists.name: Ernst Haeckel
artists.note: Illustrator. Detailed drawings of sea creatures.

artists.name: Iris van Herpen
artists.note: Fashion designer. Couture inspired by nature.

themes.research: Shells and pebbles on a beach, plants in a local park, seed heads, leaves, macro photos on your phone.
themes.test: Draw the same object at five different sizes. Print with real leaves.

themes.name: Structures and Architecture
themes.meaning: Buildings, frameworks, bridges, scaffolding: anything built, and how it holds together.
questions: What's the skeleton under the surface?
How do old and new buildings sit side by side?
How does a structure feel from inside compared to outside?
What's the gap between a plan and the real thing?

artists.name: Zaha Hadid
artists.note: Architect. Flowing, curved, futuristic buildings.

artists.name: Ian Murphy
artists.note: Mixed media. Layered drawings of buildings in ink, collage and paint.

artists.name: Bernd and Hilla Becher
artists.note: Photographers. Grids of black-and-white industrial structures.

artists.name: Rachel Whiteread
artists.note: Sculptor. Casts the empty spaces in and around buildings.

themes.research: Bridges, piers, stations, modern and old buildings in your town, cranes and scaffolding.
themes.test: Draw a building in one continuous line, then rebuild it as a small card maquette. Take rubbings of brick and metal.

themes.name: Decay and Transformation
themes.meaning: How things rust, rot, weather, break down, or change into something new.
questions: What's beautiful about something falling apart?
What does time do to a surface?
Can you speed decay up, or reverse it?
What's left behind afterwards?

artists.name: Anselm Kiefer
artists.note: Painter and sculptor. Huge textured works using lead, straw and ash.

artists.name: Alberto Burri
artists.note: Painter. Burnt plastic, sacking and cracked surfaces.

artists.name: Sam Taylor-Johnson
artists.note: Artist. Still Life, a time-lapse film of fruit rotting.

artists.name: Kurt Schwitters
artists.note: Collage made from scraps and rubbish.

artists.name: Martin Margiela
artists.note: Fashion. Deconstructed, unfinished-looking garments.

themes.research: Peeling paint, rusty seafront railings, old buildings, fruit left out for a week and photographed every day.
themes.test: Stain paper with tea, coffee or rust. Distress a surface with sandpaper or bleach (ask your tutor first).

themes.name: Place and Belonging
themes.meaning: The places that make you who you are: home, a town, a landscape, a room.
questions: What makes somewhere feel like home?
How does a place change from day to night?
What do you notice on a route you take every day?
Where do you feel you don't belong?

artists.name: Do Ho Suh
artists.note: Sculptor. Life-size see-through fabric copies of homes he's lived in.

artists.name: Kyffin Williams
artists.note: Painter. Thick palette-knife paintings of Welsh landscapes.

artists.name: Edward Hopper
artists.note: Painter. Quiet, lonely scenes of American towns and rooms.

artists.name: L.S. Lowry
artists.note: Painter. Crowds of figures in northern industrial towns.

themes.research: Your street, your bedroom, the view from your window at different times, your daily commute.
themes.test: Make a map that isn't about geography (feelings, sounds, smells). Draw one place in three kinds of weather.

themes.name: Memory and Nostalgia
themes.meaning: How we remember the past, what we keep, and what we forget.
questions: What object holds a memory for you?
How do memories fade or blur?
What does childhood look like to you now?
Whose memories do old photos keep?

artists.name: Joseph Cornell
artists.note: Small glass-fronted boxes filled with found objects.

artists.name: Christian Boltanski
artists.note: Installations of old photos, archives and lights about memory and loss.

artists.name: Louise Bourgeois
artists.note: Sculpture and fabric works drawn from childhood memories.

artists.name: Gerhard Richter
artists.note: Painter. Blurred paintings made from photographs.

themes.research: Copies of family photos, childhood objects, letters, tickets, and a family member's story about the past.
themes.test: Transfer a photo onto fabric. Fade an image by sanding it, washing it, or layering tracing paper over it.

themes.name: The Body
themes.meaning: The human figure: how it moves, what it feels, and how it's seen.
questions: What can hands alone say?
How do you show a body moving?
What if you treat the body like a landscape?
How do clothes change the shape of a body?

artists.name: Egon Schiele
artists.note: Painter. Tense, expressive line drawings of figures.

artists.name: Jenny Saville
artists.note: Painter. Huge, close-up paintings of bodies.

artists.name: Antony Gormley
artists.note: Sculptor. Figures cast from his own body.

artists.name: Ron Mueck
artists.note: Sculptor. Hyperreal figures at strange scales.

artists.name: Alexander McQueen
artists.note: Fashion. Dramatic garments that reshape the body.

themes.research: Life drawing classes, your own hands and feet, 30-second sketches of people on a bus or train.
themes.test: Fill a page with 30-second gesture drawings. Make small figures from wire or masking tape.

themes.name: The City
themes.meaning: Busy streets, crowds, signs, noise and transport: the energy of urban life.
questions: What would the sound of a city look like drawn?
What's the city like at night?
What gets overlooked: drains, signs, litter?
How do people move through a busy space?

artists.name: Stephen Wiltshire
artists.note: Draws detailed city panoramas from memory.

artists.name: Julie Mehretu
artists.note: Painter. Layered abstract works built on architectural plans.

artists.name: Jean-Michel Basquiat
artists.note: Painter. Raw, street-inspired works mixing words and images.

artists.name: Saul Leiter
artists.note: Photographer. Colourful street photos full of rain and reflections.

themes.research: Busy shopping streets, markets, stations, and signs, tickets and maps to use in collage.
themes.test: Collage with tickets, maps and receipts. Draw a scene for five minutes, then draw it again from memory.

themes.name: Hidden and Revealed
themes.meaning: What's covered, concealed or disguised, and what gets uncovered.
questions: What do people hide?
What's inside things?
What happens when you wrap or cover something?
What only appears when you look closely?

artists.name: Christo and Jeanne-Claude
artists.note: Wrapped entire buildings and landscapes in fabric.

artists.name: René Magritte
artists.note: Painter. Faces hidden behind objects, like a floating apple.

artists.name: Liu Bolin
artists.note: Paints himself so he disappears into the background.

artists.name: Doris Salcedo
artists.note: Sculptor. Furniture filled with concrete, hiding traces of loss.

themes.research: Look inside things: cut fruit, old gadgets. Photograph through windows, net curtains, fences and frosted glass.
themes.test: Layer tracing paper or wax over an image. Wrap an object and draw it. Cut windows in a page to show the one beneath.

themes.name: Boundaries and Barriers
themes.meaning: Lines that divide: fences, walls, borders, edges and rules.
questions: What separates people from each other?
Where exactly is the edge between land and sea?
Who's inside, and who's left outside?
Can a barrier be invisible?

artists.name: Mona Hatoum
artists.note: Installation. Everyday objects turned threatening, about home and borders.

artists.name: Doris Salcedo
artists.note: Shibboleth, a long crack cut into the floor of Tate Modern.

artists.name: Ai Weiwei
artists.note: Installation. Large works about migration and borders.

artists.name: Richard Serra
artists.note: Sculptor. Huge curved steel walls you walk between.

themes.research: Coastlines and riverbanks, sea walls, gates, railings and walls.
themes.test: Stitch, tape or wire across a drawing. Draw both sides of the same fence.

themes.name: Fragments
themes.meaning: Broken pieces, parts of a whole, and things put back together.
questions: What can a single piece tell you about the whole?
Can broken be beautiful?
How do you rebuild something?
What happens when you cut up and rearrange?

artists.name: Cornelia Parker
artists.note: Cold Dark Matter, a shed blown up and hung as fragments.

artists.name: Hannah Höch
artists.note: Sharp photomontages cut from magazines.

artists.name: David Hockney
artists.note: Photo "joiners": one scene built from many photos.

artists.name: Kintsugi
artists.note: Japanese craft of mending broken pottery with gold.

themes.research: Sea glass and broken shells on the beach, chipped crockery, torn posters, your own old drawings cut up.
themes.test: Build a photo joiner of one scene. Cut a drawing into strips and rearrange them.

themes.name: Light and Shadow
themes.meaning: How light shapes what we see, and what darkness hides.
questions: How do shadows change through the day?
Can a shadow be the artwork?
What's light like in different weather?
What does darkness feel like?

artists.name: Caravaggio
artists.note: Painter. Dramatic strong light and deep shadow.

artists.name: Rembrandt
artists.note: Painter. Soft, glowing light on faces.

artists.name: Olafur Eliasson
artists.note: The Weather Project, a giant artificial sun inside Tate Modern.

artists.name: Tim Noble and Sue Webster
artists.note: Piles of rubbish that cast perfect shadow portraits.

artists.name: Kara Walker
artists.note: Cut-paper silhouettes telling difficult histories.

themes.research: Shadows photographed at different times of day, a torch on objects in a dark room, light through glass and water.
themes.test: Draw only the shadows of an object. Use white chalk or charcoal on black paper.

themes.name: Pattern and Repetition
themes.meaning: Things that repeat: shapes, marks, motifs and rhythms.
questions: Where do you see repetition every day?
What happens when one thing is repeated hundreds of times?
When does a pattern become hypnotic?
What happens when you break a pattern?

artists.name: Yayoi Kusama
artists.note: Dots and repeated forms covering everything.

artists.name: William Morris
artists.note: Designer. Repeating wallpaper and fabric patterns from nature.

artists.name: Bridget Riley
artists.note: Painter. Op Art patterns that seem to move.

artists.name: Andy Warhol
artists.note: Repeated screen-printed images.

artists.name: M.C. Escher
artists.note: Printmaker. Interlocking tessellations.

themes.research: Tiles, brickwork, railings, fabric and packaging. Old buildings often have great tiled floors.
themes.test: Design a repeat tile and stamp or print it. Repeat one mark 100 times and see what it turns into.

themes.name: Water and the Coast
themes.meaning: Sea, rain, rivers, reflections and tides.
questions: How do you draw something that never stays still?
What does the sea leave behind?
How does water change light and colour?
What's it like to live by water?

artists.name: J.M.W. Turner
artists.note: Painter. Stormy, misty seas full of light.

artists.name: Hokusai
artists.note: Printmaker. The Great Wave off Kanagawa.

artists.name: Maggi Hambling
artists.note: Painter. Energetic paintings of crashing North Sea waves.

artists.name: Zaria Forman
artists.note: Huge realistic pastel drawings of ice and water.

artists.name: Hiroshi Sugimoto
artists.note: Photographer. Calm black-and-white Seascapes.

themes.research: The nearest coast, river, lake or even puddles. Film the water moving. Collect sea glass, driftwood, seaweed.
themes.test: Drop ink onto wet paper. Sprinkle salt on watercolour. Draw the horizon every day for a week.

themes.name: Journeys and Movement
themes.meaning: Travel, routes, motion and change, from a daily commute to a whole life.
questions: How do you show movement in a still image?
What's your daily route really like?
What do you see from a train window?
Where do journeys start and end?

artists.name: Eadweard Muybridge
artists.note: Photographer. Photo sequences showing how bodies move.

artists.name: Giacomo Balla
artists.note: Futurist painter. Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash.

artists.name: Richard Long
artists.note: Land artist. A Line Made by Walking.

artists.name: Alexander Calder
artists.note: Sculptor. Hanging mobiles that move with the air.

themes.research: Your daily commute: photos, sketches, tickets, the view. Your route on a map. Slow-shutter phone photos.
themes.test: Draw on a moving bus or train. Make a sequence of drawings like frames of a film.

themes.name: Objects and Collections
themes.meaning: Everyday things, and what our stuff says about us.
questions: What do you collect, and why?
What makes an ordinary object special?
What happens when an everyday object becomes giant?
What's in your bag right now?

artists.name: Giorgio Morandi
artists.note: Painter. Quiet still lifes of the same bottles and jars.

artists.name: Michael Craig-Martin
artists.note: Bold outline drawings of everyday objects in bright colour.

artists.name: Claes Oldenburg
artists.note: Sculptor. Giant sculptures of everyday things.

artists.name: Mark Dion
artists.note: Installation. Cabinets of curiosity full of collected objects.

themes.research: The contents of your bag or pockets, charity shop finds, and local museum collections of everyday life.
themes.test: Draw one object from five angles. Arrange a collection and photograph it from above.

artists.name: Ai Weiwei
artists.known_for: Huge installations about freedom, migration and the value of everyday objects.
artists.key_work: Sunflower Seeds, 2010: 100 million hand-painted porcelain seeds at Tate Modern.
artists.borrow: Repeat one small handmade object hundreds of times.

artists.name: Anni Albers
artists.known_for: Bauhaus weaver who turned weaving into modern abstract art.
artists.key_work: Geometric woven wall hangings from the 1920s onwards.
artists.borrow: Weave paper strips or yarn into a geometric grid.

artists.name: El Anatsui
artists.known_for: Shimmering metal 'cloths' made from thousands of bottle tops joined with wire.
artists.key_work: Huge wall hangings that fold and drape like fabric.
artists.borrow: Join small found pieces with wire to make a flexible surface.

artists.name: Giacomo Balla
artists.known_for: Showed speed and movement by repeating shapes, like frames of a film.
artists.key_work: Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash, 1912.
artists.borrow: Repeat the outline of a moving thing in overlapping positions.

artists.name: Banksy
artists.known_for: Sharp, funny stencilled street art with a political message.
artists.borrow: Cut a stencil and spray or sponge it in layers.

artists.name: Jean-Michel Basquiat
artists.known_for: Raw, energetic paintings mixing words, crowns, skulls and scribbles.
artists.borrow: Mix crossed-out words and quick drawings on one layered surface.

artists.name: Bernd and Hilla Becher
artists.known_for: Black-and-white photos of industrial structures, shown in neat grids.
artists.key_work: Their 'typologies' of water towers and blast furnaces.
artists.borrow: Photograph many versions of one type of thing and display them in a grid.

artists.name: Karl Blossfeldt
artists.known_for: Sharp close-up photos of plants that look like sculpture or ironwork.
artists.key_work: Urformen der Kunst (Art Forms in Nature), 1928.
artists.borrow: Photograph a plant really close up against a plain background.

artists.name: Christian Boltanski
artists.known_for: Moving installations of old photographs, clothes and lights about memory and loss.
artists.key_work: Rooms of found photos lit by small lamps.
artists.borrow: Display old photos with light so they feel like a memorial.

artists.name: Louise Bourgeois
artists.known_for: Very personal work drawn from her childhood, including giant spiders and fabric pieces.
artists.borrow: Stitch, stuff or sculpt something that stands for a memory.

artists.name: Alberto Burri
artists.known_for: Used torn sacking, burnt plastic and cracked surfaces instead of paint.
artists.borrow: Build a surface from torn, burnt or patched materials (ask your tutor first).

artists.name: Alexander Calder
artists.known_for: Invented the mobile: hanging sculptures that move with the air.
artists.key_work: His hanging mobiles of painted metal shapes.
artists.borrow: Make a balancing mobile from wire and card shapes.

artists.name: Caravaggio
artists.known_for: Dramatic strong light and deep shadow (chiaroscuro).
artists.borrow: Light an object with one lamp in a dark room and draw it.

artists.name: Christo and Jeanne-Claude
artists.known_for: Wrapped whole buildings, bridges and coastlines in fabric for a short time.
artists.borrow: Wrap an object in fabric or paper and draw what's left.

artists.name: Joseph Cornell
artists.known_for: Small glass-fronted boxes filled with found objects, like tiny dream worlds.
artists.key_work: His shadow boxes from the 1930s to 1960s.
artists.borrow: Arrange found objects inside a small box.

artists.name: Michael Craig-Martin
artists.known_for: Bold black outlines of everyday objects in bright, flat colours.
artists.key_work: An Oak Tree, 1973: a glass of water on a shelf.
artists.borrow: Draw everyday objects in clean outline and fill them with flat colour.

artists.name: Salvador Dalí
artists.known_for: Strange dream-like paintings, like melting clocks.
artists.borrow: Combine two things that don't belong together.

artists.name: Sonia Delaunay
artists.known_for: Bright colour circles and shapes across paintings, fabric and fashion.
artists.key_work: Her 'simultaneous' textiles and clothes from the 1920s.
artists.borrow: Turn a colour study into a fabric design.

artists.name: Mark Dion
artists.known_for: Collects, sorts and displays objects like a museum cabinet of curiosities.
artists.key_work: Tate Thames Dig, 1999: objects found on the Thames foreshore.
artists.borrow: Collect, label and display objects from one place.

artists.name: Olafur Eliasson
artists.known_for: Uses light, water and weather to change how you experience a space.
artists.key_work: The Weather Project, 2003: a giant artificial sun at Tate Modern.
artists.borrow: Play with light through water, mirrors or coloured film.

artists.name: Tracey Emin
artists.known_for: Very personal work in neon, embroidery, drawing and installation.
artists.borrow: Stitch or write your own words onto fabric.

artists.name: M.C. Escher
artists.known_for: Mind-bending tessellations and impossible buildings.
artists.borrow: Design a shape that tessellates and repeat it.

artists.name: Zaria Forman
artists.known_for: Huge, realistic pastel drawings of ice and water, made after visiting the polar regions.
artists.key_work: Large drawings of icebergs and waves.
artists.borrow: Blend soft pastel with your fingers for water and ice.

artists.name: Andy Goldsworthy
artists.known_for: Temporary sculptures made in nature from leaves, ice, stone and sticks.
artists.key_work: The film Rivers and Tides, 2001, shows him at work.
artists.borrow: Arrange natural materials outdoors and photograph them.

artists.name: Antony Gormley
artists.known_for: Figures based on casts of his own body, often in public spaces.
artists.borrow: Trace or cast your own body as a starting point.

artists.name: Zaha Hadid
artists.known_for: Flowing, curved, futuristic buildings.
artists.borrow: Draw a building made only of sweeping curves.

artists.name: Ernst Haeckel
artists.known_for: Detailed, symmetrical drawings of sea creatures and tiny life forms.
artists.key_work: Kunstformen der Natur (Art Forms in Nature), 1904.
artists.borrow: Draw a natural object with careful symmetry and fine detail.

artists.name: Maggi Hambling
artists.known_for: Energetic, gestural paintings of crashing waves.
artists.key_work: Scallop, 2003, a steel sculpture on Aldeburgh beach.
artists.borrow: Paint water fast with big, loose brush marks.

artists.name: Mona Hatoum
artists.known_for: Everyday objects turned uneasy or threatening, about home and borders.
artists.key_work: Hot Spot, 2013: a glowing red neon globe.
artists.borrow: Change one thing about a familiar object to make it unsettling.

artists.name: Barbara Hepworth
artists.known_for: Smooth, organic sculptures pierced with holes.
artists.key_work: Her garden and studio in St Ives is now a museum.
artists.borrow: Carve or model a smooth form with a hole through it.

artists.name: Lubaina Himid
artists.known_for: Bold, colourful work about Black history and identity. Won the Turner Prize in 2017.
artists.key_work: Naming the Money, 2004: 100 painted cut-out figures.
artists.borrow: Use pattern and colour to tell a story about people.

artists.name: Hannah Höch
artists.known_for: Sharp, funny photomontages cut from magazines.
artists.borrow: Make a photomontage from magazine cuttings.

artists.name: David Hockney
artists.known_for: Bright paintings, iPad drawings and photo 'joiners' built from many photos.
artists.borrow: Build one scene from lots of overlapping photos.

artists.name: Katsushika Hokusai
artists.known_for: Woodblock prints of waves, mountains and everyday life.
artists.key_work: The Great Wave off Kanagawa, about 1831.
artists.borrow: Simplify water into bold, curling shapes.

artists.name: Edward Hopper
artists.known_for: Quiet, lonely scenes of cities, diners and rooms.
artists.borrow: Paint an empty or lonely space with strong light.

artists.name: Gwen John
artists.known_for: Quiet portraits and interiors in soft, muted colours. Born in Haverfordwest.
artists.key_work: A Corner of the Artist's Room in Paris, about 1907–09.
artists.borrow: Paint a quiet corner of a room in a limited palette.

artists.name: Frida Kahlo
artists.known_for: Self-portraits full of personal symbols about pain, identity and heritage.
artists.borrow: Surround a self-portrait with objects that mean something to you.

artists.name: Wassily Kandinsky
artists.known_for: One of the first abstract painters. Linked colour and shape to music.
artists.borrow: Paint what a piece of music looks like.

artists.name: Anish Kapoor
artists.known_for: Huge mirror-polished and deep-coloured sculptures that play with space.
artists.borrow: Use reflective surfaces to distort a space.

artists.name: Rei Kawakubo
artists.known_for: Founded Comme des Garçons. Strange, sculptural, deconstructed clothes.
artists.key_work: Her 1997 collection with padded lumps on the body.
artists.borrow: Change a garment's silhouette with padding or odd shapes.

artists.name: Anselm Kiefer
artists.known_for: Huge, heavily textured works using lead, straw, ash and plaster.
artists.key_work: Large landscape paintings thick with real materials.
artists.borrow: Mix sand, PVA or plaster into paint for texture.

artists.name: Gustav Klimt
artists.known_for: Rich decorative pattern and real gold leaf.
artists.borrow: Fill clothing or background areas with decorative pattern.

artists.name: Yayoi Kusama
artists.known_for: Dots and repeated forms covering everything, including Infinity Mirror Rooms.
artists.borrow: Cover an object or space completely in one repeated mark.

artists.name: Dorothea Lange
artists.known_for: Documentary photos of people living through hard times.
artists.borrow: Take portraits that tell a story about someone's life.

artists.name: Saul Leiter
artists.known_for: Colourful street photos full of rain, reflections and blur.
artists.key_work: His colour street photos of New York from the 1950s.
artists.borrow: Photograph a street through a wet or steamy window.

artists.name: Liu Bolin
artists.known_for: Paints himself to blend into backgrounds, then photographs it.
artists.key_work: His Hiding in the City series.
artists.borrow: Camouflage an object so it disappears into its background.

artists.name: Richard Long
artists.known_for: Art made by walking: lines, circles and maps of journeys.
artists.borrow: Record a walk with photos, maps and collected objects.

artists.name: L.S. Lowry
artists.known_for: Crowds of thin 'matchstick' figures in northern industrial towns.
artists.borrow: Draw a busy crowd with simple, repeated figures.

artists.name: René Magritte
artists.known_for: Everyday things made strange: hidden faces, floating apples, pipes that aren't pipes.
artists.borrow: Hide part of a portrait behind an unexpected object.

artists.name: Martin Margiela
artists.known_for: Deconstructed clothes that look unfinished or turned inside out.
artists.borrow: Take a garment apart and put it back together differently.

artists.name: Henri Matisse
artists.known_for: Bright colour, and late in life 'drawing with scissors' using paper cut-outs.
artists.borrow: Cut shapes straight from painted paper with no drawing first.

artists.name: Alexander McQueen
artists.known_for: Dramatic, theatrical clothes that reshape the body, often inspired by nature.
artists.borrow: Design a garment inspired by a natural form.

artists.name: Julie Mehretu
artists.known_for: Huge layered abstract paintings built on architectural plans and maps.
artists.key_work: Large paintings layering city plans with energetic marks.
artists.borrow: Layer maps or plans with fast marks on top.

artists.name: Issey Miyake
artists.known_for: Famous for pleated fabric that moves with the body.
artists.borrow: Experiment with pleating and folding fabric or paper.

artists.name: Piet Mondrian
artists.known_for: Grids of black lines with blocks of red, yellow and blue.
artists.key_work: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930.
artists.borrow: Simplify a view down to lines and blocks of colour.

artists.name: Claude Monet
artists.known_for: Painted changing light and weather, often the same scene again and again.
artists.borrow: Paint the same view at different times of day.

artists.name: Henry Moore
artists.known_for: Large, smooth reclining figures inspired by bones, stones and landscape.
artists.borrow: Turn a figure into simple, rounded forms.

artists.name: Giorgio Morandi
artists.known_for: Quiet still lifes of the same bottles and jars, in soft dusty colours.
artists.key_work: Still lifes painted over many decades.
artists.borrow: Paint a few simple objects in a muted palette.

artists.name: William Morris
artists.known_for: Repeating wallpaper and fabric patterns based on plants and birds.
artists.borrow: Turn plant drawings into a repeating pattern.

artists.name: Ron Mueck
artists.known_for: Hyperreal human figures at strange sizes, either huge or tiny.
artists.borrow: Change the scale of something realistic to make it strange.

artists.name: Edvard Munch
artists.known_for: Expressive paintings about anxiety, love and fear.
artists.borrow: Use colour and swirling line to show a feeling.

artists.name: Ian Murphy
artists.known_for: Layered drawings of buildings in ink, collage, paint and charcoal.
artists.key_work: Mixed-media drawings of cities and architecture.
artists.borrow: Draw a building over a collaged, inky background.

artists.name: Eadweard Muybridge
artists.known_for: Photo sequences that showed how people and animals move.
artists.borrow: Shoot a movement as a sequence of photos.

artists.name: Louise Nevelson
artists.known_for: Wall sculptures of wooden scraps in boxes, all painted one colour.
artists.borrow: Paint a collection of scraps one colour to unify them.

artists.name: Tim Noble and Sue Webster
artists.known_for: Piles of rubbish that cast perfect shadow portraits when lit.
artists.borrow: Arrange objects so their shadow makes a picture.

artists.name: Chris Ofili
artists.known_for: Rich, layered paintings using glitter, collage and resin. Won the Turner Prize in 1998.
artists.borrow: Build a painting up in decorative layers.

artists.name: Georgia O'Keeffe
artists.known_for: Huge close-up flowers, bones and desert landscapes.
artists.borrow: Paint something small at a huge, close-up scale.

artists.name: Claes Oldenburg
artists.known_for: Giant sculptures of everyday objects, often with Coosje van Bruggen.
artists.borrow: Make an everyday object huge, or soft.

artists.name: Cornelia Parker
artists.known_for: Destroys objects, then hangs the pieces in the air.
artists.key_work: Cold Dark Matter: An Exploded View, 1991.
artists.borrow: Suspend fragments on thread to rebuild an object in space.

artists.name: Grayson Perry
artists.known_for: Pots and tapestries about class, taste and identity. Won the Turner Prize in 2003.
artists.borrow: Decorate a form with images that tell your story.

artists.name: Pablo Picasso
artists.known_for: Co-invented Cubism, showing many viewpoints at once.
artists.borrow: Draw an object from several angles in one picture.

artists.name: Jackson Pollock
artists.known_for: Dripped and poured paint onto canvas laid on the floor.
artists.borrow: Make marks with your whole arm by dripping or flicking.

artists.name: Robert Rauschenberg
artists.known_for: 'Combines' that mixed painting with real objects and printed images.
artists.borrow: Attach real objects to a painted surface.

artists.name: Paula Rego
artists.known_for: Powerful, story-like pictures of women, often based on fairy tales.
artists.borrow: Stage a scene with people or props, then draw it.

artists.name: Rembrandt van Rijn
artists.known_for: Glowing light on faces and honest self-portraits.
artists.borrow: Draw a self-portrait lit from one side.

artists.name: Gerhard Richter
artists.known_for: Blurred paintings from photos, and huge squeegee-dragged abstracts.
artists.borrow: Paint from a photo, then blur it while it's wet.

artists.name: Bridget Riley
artists.known_for: Op Art patterns of lines and shapes that seem to move.
artists.borrow: Gradually change a repeated shape to create movement.

artists.name: Mark Rothko
artists.known_for: Big soft-edged blocks of colour meant to create strong feelings.
artists.key_work: The Seagram Murals, now at Tate.
artists.borrow: Layer thin washes of colour to create a mood.

artists.name: Doris Salcedo
artists.known_for: Quiet, powerful work about loss, using furniture and concrete.
artists.key_work: Shibboleth, 2007: a crack in the floor of Tate Modern.
artists.borrow: Fill or block part of an object to change its meaning.

artists.name: Jenny Saville
artists.known_for: Huge, fleshy, close-up paintings of bodies.
artists.borrow: Paint skin with thick, expressive brushwork.

artists.name: Elsa Schiaparelli
artists.known_for: Playful surrealist fashion, made with artists like Dalí.
artists.borrow: Put an unexpected object or image onto a garment.

artists.name: Egon Schiele
artists.known_for: Tense, twisting, expressive line drawings of figures.
artists.borrow: Draw a figure with sharp, angular, confident lines.

artists.name: Kurt Schwitters
artists.known_for: Made 'Merz' collages from tickets, wrappers and rubbish.
artists.borrow: Collage with tickets and packaging you've collected.

artists.name: Richard Serra
artists.known_for: Huge curved steel walls that you walk around and between.
artists.borrow: Make a card model of walls that change how you move.

artists.name: Cindy Sherman
artists.known_for: Photographs herself dressed as invented characters.
artists.borrow: Photograph yourself as a character you've invented.

artists.name: Yinka Shonibare
artists.known_for: Uses colourful Dutch wax print fabric to question history and culture.
artists.borrow: Cover a familiar shape in a fabric that changes its meaning.

artists.name: Hiroshi Sugimoto
artists.known_for: Calm, minimal black-and-white photos of the sea and horizon.
artists.borrow: Photograph the horizon split exactly in half.

artists.name: Do Ho Suh
artists.known_for: Life-size see-through fabric copies of homes he's lived in.
artists.borrow: Recreate part of your home in thin fabric or tracing paper.

artists.name: Sam Taylor-Johnson
artists.known_for: Photography and film about time, change and the body.
artists.key_work: Still Life, 2001: a time-lapse film of fruit rotting.
artists.borrow: Photograph the same object every day as it changes.

artists.name: J.M.W. Turner
artists.known_for: Stormy, misty seas and skies full of light.
artists.key_work: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth, 1842.
artists.borrow: Paint weather with loose, swirling washes.

artists.name: James Turrell
artists.known_for: Rooms and spaces where light itself is the artwork.
artists.key_work: Roden Crater, a long-running project in Arizona.
artists.borrow: Make a box that frames light or sky.

artists.name: Vincent van Gogh
artists.known_for: Thick, swirling brushstrokes and expressive colour.
artists.borrow: Use directional brush marks to show movement and feeling.

artists.name: Iris van Herpen
artists.known_for: Couture inspired by nature and science, often using 3D printing.
artists.borrow: Build a garment surface from repeated natural shapes.

artists.name: Kara Walker
artists.known_for: Cut-paper silhouettes that tell difficult stories about history.
artists.borrow: Tell a story using only black silhouettes.

artists.name: Andy Warhol
artists.known_for: Repeated screen-printed images of celebrities and products.
artists.borrow: Repeat one image several times in different colours.

artists.name: Vivienne Westwood
artists.known_for: Brought punk into fashion, mixing tartan, history and rebellion.
artists.borrow: Rip, pin and rework a traditional fabric.

artists.name: Rachel Whiteread
artists.known_for: Casts the empty space in and around objects and buildings.
artists.key_work: House, 1993: a cast of the inside of a London house.
artists.borrow: Cast the inside of a box or container in plaster.

artists.name: Kehinde Wiley
artists.known_for: Puts modern sitters into grand poses from old portraits, with bold patterned backgrounds.
artists.borrow: Pose someone like an old portrait and add a patterned background.

artists.name: Kyffin Williams
artists.known_for: Thick palette-knife paintings of Welsh landscapes and people.
artists.key_work: His paintings of Snowdonia and Anglesey.
artists.borrow: Paint a landscape with a palette knife instead of a brush.

artists.name: Stephen Wiltshire
artists.known_for: Detailed city panoramas drawn from memory, often after one short look.
artists.key_work: His panoramic drawings of cities like London and New York.
artists.borrow: Look at a view for one minute, then draw it from memory.
